slides.teach: Know the reason this control exists and the security objective it supports.
defs: Dividing a network into controlled zones to limit access and lateral movement.

course.learn: Access control restricts which subjects can access which resources and what actions they may perform. ACLs express allow/deny rules on objects, interfaces, or network traffic.
course.why: Access control enforces least privilege and prevents an authenticated user from automatically reaching every resource.
course.example: A router ACL allows HTTPS from the public Internet to a web server but denies administrative ports.
course.exam: Authentication proves identity; access control/authorization limits actions. ACLs are rule lists that enforce those decisions.

Network segmentation separates systems into different trust zones so traffic must cross controlled boundaries. VLANs, subnets, ACLs, and firewalls are common mechanisms.

course.learn: Permissions define the actions a subject may perform on a resource, such as read, write, execute, modify, or administer. They are one mechanism used to implement authorization.
course.why: Correct permissions enforce least privilege and protect both confidentiality and integrity.
course.example: A finance analyst can read reports but cannot change the application binaries or security configuration.
course.exam: Do not give broad administrator/full-control rights when a narrower permission set satisfies the task.
